claim: Choanoflagellates are the closest living relatives of animals.
source: The closest living relatives of animals, the choanoflagellates (Ruiz-Trillo et al., 2008; King et al., 2008), have been thought to exist solely in a flagellate form (except while encysted [Leadbeater, 2015]).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ruiz-Trillo et al., 2008 and King et al., 2008

claim: Choanoflagellates have been thought to exist solely in a flagellate form except while encysted.
source: The closest living relatives of animals, the choanoflagellates (Ruiz-Trillo et al., 2008; King et al., 2008), have been thought to exist solely in a flagellate form (except while encysted [Leadbeater, 2015]).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leadbeater, 2015

claim: Choanoflagellates subjected to confinement become amoeboid by retracting their flagella and activating myosin-based motility.
source: Here, we show that choanoflagellates subjected to confinement become amoeboid by retracting their flagella and activating myosin-based motility.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figures 1-4 and Videos 1-9

claim: The amoeboid switch in choanoflagellates allows escape from confinement.
source: This switch allows escape from confinement and is conserved across choanoflagellate diversity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing escape behavior

claim: The amoeboid switch is conserved across choanoflagellate diversity.
source: This switch allows escape from confinement and is conserved across choanoflagellate diversity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing multiple choanoflagellate species

claim: Amoeboid cell motility is central to animal development.
source: Amoeboid (or crawling) cell motility is central to several key aspects of animal biology, including development (Kardash et al., 2010; Barton et al., 2016), immunity (Kopf et al., 2020; Reversat et al., 2020), and wound healing (Lamouille et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kardash et al., 2010 and Barton et al., 2016

claim: Amoeboid cell motility is central to animal immunity.
source: Amoeboid (or crawling) cell motility is central to several key aspects of animal biology, including development (Kardash et al., 2010; Barton et al., 2016), immunity (Kopf et al., 2020; Reversat et al., 2020), and wound healing (Lamouille et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kopf et al., 2020 and Reversat et al., 2020

claim: Amoeboid cell motility is central to animal wound healing.
source: Amoeboid (or crawling) cell motility is central to several key aspects of animal biology, including development (Kardash et al., 2010; Barton et al., 2016), immunity (Kopf et al., 2020; Reversat et al., 2020), and wound healing (Lamouille et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lamouille et al., 2014

claim: Haeckel proposed in 1874 that animals descended from amoebae that evolved coloniality and later acquired cilia.
source: Haeckel originally proposed in 1874 that animals descended from amoebae that evolved coloniality and later acquired cilia (Haeckel, 1874).
evidence: Supported by citation to Haeckel, 1874

claim: Metchnikoff proposed in 1886 that animals originated from colonies of flagellated cells resembling modern choanoflagellates.
source: In contrast, Metchnikoff proposed in 1886 that animals originated from colonies of flagellated cells resembling modern choanoflagellates (Metchnikoff, 1886), a view that was incorporated into later interpretations of Haeckel's Gastraea hypothesis (Nielsen, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Metchnikoff, 1886

claim: Naegleria alternates between a flagellate and an amoeboid form.
source: An intermediate view (Willmer, 1971) was inspired by the discovery of protozoans such as Naegleria, which alternate between a flagellate and an amoeboid form (Schardinger, 1899; Fulton, 1977).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schardinger, 1899 and Fulton, 1977

claim: Naegleria belongs to branches of the tree of life that are far removed from animals.
source: Subsequent phylogenetic analyses revealed that protozoans known to alternate between flagellate and amoeboid forms (such as Naegleria) belonged to branches of the tree of life that were far removed from animals (Fritz-Laylin et al., 2010), making their relevance to animal origins uncertain.
evidence: Supported by citation to Fritz-Laylin et al., 2010

claim: A single report of a colonial choanoflagellate containing both flagellated and amoeboid cells appeared in 1882 but was never corroborated.
source: A single report of a colonial choanoflagellate containing both flagellated and amoeboid cells appeared in 1882 (Kent, 1882), but was never corroborated (Leadbeater, 2015), raising questions about its validity.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kent, 1882 and Leadbeater, 2015

claim: The diagnostic cell architecture of choanoflagellates is that of a seemingly rigid, ovoid cell bearing an apical collar complex.
source: Instead, the diagnostic and seemingly universal cell architecture of choanoflagellates is that of a seemingly rigid, ovoid cell bearing an apical collar complex – a single flagellum surrounded by a microvillar collar.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about choanoflagellate morphology

claim: Some close outgroups to choanoflagellates and animals produce amoeboid cells.
source: However, modern choanoflagellates doubtless differ in some respects from their last common ancestor with animals (Sogabe et al., 2019) and some close outgroups to choanoflagellates and animals produce amoeboid cells (Ruiz-Trillo et al., 2008; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2017; Suga and Ruiz-Trillo, 2013; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2013b; Fritz-Laylin, 2020) or alternate flagellate and amoeboid forms (Hehenberger et al., 2017; Tikhonenkov et al., 2020; Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017b), raising the possibility that the cellular machinery for cell crawling and flagellar swimming both predate the divergence of the choanoflagellate and animal lineages (Arendt et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including Ruiz-Trillo et al., 2008; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2017; Suga and Ruiz-Trillo, 2013; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2013b; Fritz-Laylin, 2020

claim: Some close outgroups to choanoflagellates and animals alternate flagellate and amoeboid forms.
source: However, modern choanoflagellates doubtless differ in some respects from their last common ancestor with animals (Sogabe et al., 2019) and some close outgroups to choanoflagellates and animals produce amoeboid cells (Ruiz-Trillo et al., 2008; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2017; Suga and Ruiz-Trillo, 2013; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2013b; Fritz-Laylin, 2020) or alternate flagellate and amoeboid forms (Hehenberger et al., 2017; Tikhonenkov et al., 2020; Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017b), raising the possibility that the cellular machinery for cell crawling and flagellar swimming both predate the divergence of the choanoflagellate and animal lineages (Arendt et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hehenberger et al., 2017; Tikhonenkov et al., 2020; Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017b

claim: Filopodia are slender, finger-like protrusions containing bundles of actin filaments found in animal cells, choanoflagellates, and filastereans.
source: These include cellular protrusions frequently involved in locomotion: (1) filopodia: slender, finger-like protrusions containing bundles of actin filaments, which are found in animals cells, choanoflagellates, and filastereans (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2013a);
evidence: Supported by citation to Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2013a

claim: Pseudopods are broad, flat protrusions containing branched F-actin networks reticulated by the Arp2/3 complex.
source: (2) pseudopods: broad, flat protrusions containing branched F-actin networks reticulated by the Arp2/3 complex downstream of the actin regulators SCAR and WASP, which are observed in mammalian neutrophils and chytrid fungi (Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017b);
evidence: Supported by citation to Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017b

claim: Blebs are round protrusions devoid of F-actin which form by delamination of the plasma membrane from the actomyosin cortex.
source: (3) blebs: round protrusions devoid of F-actin which form by delamination of the plasma membrane from the actomyosin cortex under the influence of actin/myosin II cortex contractility.
evidence: Based on established cell biological knowledge

claim: Blebs have been observed in mammalian macrophages and zebrafish primordial germ cells.
source: Blebs have been observed in animal cells (such as mammalian macrophages and zebrafish primordial germ cells) and in free-living amoebae such as Entamoeba histolytica and Dictyostelium discoideum (reviewed in Paluch and Raz, 2013 and Charras and Paluch, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Paluch and Raz, 2013 and Charras and Paluch, 2008

claim: Blebs have been observed in Entamoeba histolytica and Dictyostelium discoideum.
source: Blebs have been observed in animal cells (such as mammalian macrophages and zebrafish primordial germ cells) and in free-living amoebae such as Entamoeba histolytica and Dictyostelium discoideum (reviewed in Paluch and Raz, 2013 and Charras and Paluch, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Paluch and Raz, 2013 and Charras and Paluch, 2008

claim: Choanoflagellate genomes encode predicted regulators of pseudopod formation (Arp2/3, SCAR, and WASP).
source: For example, even though neither blebs nor locomotory pseudopods had previously been observed in choanoflagellates, choanoflagellate genomes encode predicted regulators of pseudopod formation (Arp2/3, SCAR, and WASP) and of blebbing (F-actin and myosin II).
evidence: Based on genomic data

claim: Choanoflagellate genomes encode predicted regulators of blebbing (F-actin and myosin II).
source: For example, even though neither blebs nor locomotory pseudopods had previously been observed in choanoflagellates, choanoflagellate genomes encode predicted regulators of pseudopod formation (Arp2/3, SCAR, and WASP) and of blebbing (F-actin and myosin II).
evidence: Based on genomic data

claim: In choanoflagellates, Arp2/3, SCAR, and WASP have been proposed to mediate the formation of phagocytic cups.
source: In choanoflagellates, Arp2/3, SCAR, and WASP have been proposed to mediate the formation of phagocytic cups, which are involved in feeding and might be structurally similar to pseudopods, but do not contribute to locomotion (Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017b

claim: The actin/myosin II complex underlies the formation of the cytokinetic ring that mediates sister-cell separation during cell division in yeasts and mammals.
source: Similarly, the actin/myosin II complex not only is involved in blebbing but also underlies the formation of the cytokinetic ring that mediates sister-cell separation during cell division in multiple opisthokonts, including in yeasts and mammals (Pollard and Wu, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pollard and Wu, 2010

claim: Physical confinement regulates amoeboid cell differentiation and crawling motility in zebrafish embryonic cells.
source: Although amoeboid cells had not previously been reported in choanoflagellates, physical confinement regulates amoeboid cell differentiation and crawling motility in a wide range of eukaryotic cells, including zebrafish embryonic cells (Ruprecht et al., 2015), mammalian mesenchymal cells (Liu et al., 2015), some chytrid fungi (Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017b), dictyostelid amoebae (Srivastava et al., 2020), and euglenoid algae (Noselli et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ruprecht et al., 2015

claim: Physical confinement regulates amoeboid cell differentiation and crawling motility in mammalian mesenchymal cells.
source: Although amoeboid cells had not previously been reported in choanoflagellates, physical confinement regulates amoeboid cell differentiation and crawling motility in a wide range of eukaryotic cells, including zebrafish embryonic cells (Ruprecht et al., 2015), mammalian mesenchymal cells (Liu et al., 2015), some chytrid fungi (Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017b), dictyostelid amoebae (Srivastava et al., 2020), and euglenoid algae (Noselli et al., 2019).

claim: Single cells of S. rosetta confined in a space of 4 μm or more maintained the canonical flagellate phenotype.
source: Single cells of S. rosetta confined in a space of 4 μm or more maintained the canonical flagellate phenotype, consistent with the cell body not being deformed (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D

claim: Confinement below 3 μm elicited an active response from S. rosetta cells, which started dynamically extending and retracting protrusions within a few seconds.
source: On the other hand, confinement below 3 μm elicited an active response from the cells, which started dynamically extending and retracting protrusions within a few seconds (Figure 1B–D; Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D and Figure 1—video 1

claim: In 2 μm confinement or less, most S. rosetta cells retracted their flagellum within minutes.
source: In 2 μm confinement or less, most cells retracted their flagellum within minutes, thus acquiring a fully amoeboid phenotype (Figure 1B–J; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 1—video 1

claim: Releasing confinement fully reversed the phenotypic switch in S. rosetta.
source: Releasing confinement fully reversed the phenotypic switch (Figure 1K–P).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K-P

claim: Newly unconfined S. rosetta cells retracted their dynamic protrusions, regained a round shape, and regrew a flagellum close to the position of the original, retracted one.
source: Newly unconfined cells retracted their dynamic protrusions, regained a round shape, and regrew a flagellum close to the position of the original, retracted one (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D; Figure 1—video 2), suggesting that information on apicobasal cell polarity is conserved in the amoeboid form, though not externally visible.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D and Figure 1—video 2

claim: Information on apicobasal cell polarity is conserved in the amoeboid form of S. rosetta, though not externally visible.
source: Newly unconfined cells retracted their dynamic protrusions, regained a round shape, and regrew a flagellum close to the position of the original, retracted one (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D; Figure 1—video 2), suggesting that information on apicobasal cell polarity is conserved in the amoeboid form, though not externally visible.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the flagellum regenerates in approximately the same position

claim: S. rosetta rosette cells became amoeboid under 2 μm confinement.
source: Both these cell types also differentiated into amoeboid cells with dynamic protrusions under confinement, showing that competence to undergo the amoeboid switch is not restricted to a single S. rosetta cell phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: S. rosetta thecate cells became amoeboid under 2 μm confinement.
source: Both these cell types also differentiated into amoeboid cells with dynamic protrusions under confinement, showing that competence to undergo the amoeboid switch is not restricted to a single S. rosetta cell phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: S. rosetta responded in the same way to every type of confined environment tested.
source: Finally, S. rosetta responded in the same way to every type of confined environment tested, including the pressure-controlled dynamic cell confiner (Figure 1A,C,D), glass coverslips separated by microbeads, which served as spacers (Video 2), thin liquid films spread under a layer of oxygen-permeant oil (Video 3), and agar gels (Video 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,C,D and Videos 2-4

claim: The amoeboid switch in S. rosetta is induced by cell deformation itself, independent of the properties of the substrate.
source: This suggests that the amoeboid switch is induced by cell deformation itself, independent of the properties of the substrate.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that S. rosetta responds the same way to different types of confinement

claim: Inhibition of actin polymerization with latrunculin B prevented the formation of cell protrusions in S. rosetta.
source: We found that inhibition of actin polymerization with latrunculin B prevented the formation of cell protrusions in S. rosetta (Figure 2B), thus implicating F-actin in their formation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Inhibition of the Arp2/3 complex with CK666 did not prevent formation of S. rosetta cell protrusions.
source: Inhibition of the Arp2/3 complex with CK666 did not prevent formation of S. rosetta cell protrusions, suggesting they might represent blebs rather than pseudopods (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Treatment with the myosin II inhibitor blebbistatin reduced the formation of cell protrusions in S. rosetta.
source: The inference that these protrusions are blebs was independently demonstrated by disruption of actomyosin contractility by treatment with the myosin II inhibitor blebbistatin, which reduced the formation of cell protrusions (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: In animal cells, nascent and expanding blebs are initially devoid of F-actin, which then re-invades the blebs before retraction.
source: In animal cells, nascent and expanding blebs are initially devoid of F-actin, which then re-invades the blebs before retraction (Charras et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Charras et al., 2006

claim: F-actin dynamics in S. rosetta cell protrusions resembled those seen in blebbing animal cells.
source: To investigate the localization and behavior of F-actin in cell protrusions, we generated a transgenic strain of S. rosetta expressing LifeAct-mCherry (Booth et al., 2018) and observed F-actin dynamics in the protrusions of confined cells that resembled those seen in blebbing animal cells (Figure 2C–K; Figure 3; Videos 5–7).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-K, Figure 3, and Videos 5-7

claim: Fixed confined S. rosetta cells showed both F-actin-free and F-actin-encased protrusions, consistent with expanding and retracting blebs.
source: Again, we observed both F-actin-free and F-actin-encased protrusions, consistent with our observations of expanding and retracting blebs, respectively (Figure 2L–S).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2L-S

claim: Bleb formation in animal cells depends upon the contractile activity of myosin II.
source: Bleb formation in animal cells depends upon the contractile activity of myosin II (Paluch and Raz, 2013), which co-localizes with actin in the cell cortex and within retracting blebs (Charras et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Paluch and Raz, 2013 and Charras et al., 2006

claim: In unconfined flagellate S. rosetta cells, MRLC-mTFP was diffusely distributed in the cytoplasm, while also forming a few cortical patches, most frequently at the basal pole of the cell.
source: In unconfined flagellate cells, MRLC-mTFP was diffusely distributed in the cytoplasm, while also forming a few cortical patches, most frequently at the basal pole of the cell (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Under 1 μm confinement, MRLC-mTFP redistributed in less than a minute into discrete foci and fibers, both cortical and cytoplasmic.
source: Under 1 μm confinement, MRLC-mTFP redistributed in less than a minute into discrete foci and fibers, both cortical and cytoplasmic (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Confinement resulted in an increase in the cortical fraction of myosin II in S. rosetta cells.
source: Quantification of fluorescence showed that this resulted in an increase in the cortical fraction of myosin II in confined cells (Figure 4C; Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), similar to the confinement-induced redistribution of myosin to the cortex described in Dictyostelium (Srivastava et al., 2020) and vertebrate cells (Lomakin et al., 2020; Venturini et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, 4D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C

claim: In S. rosetta cells that were only confined over part of their area, myosin II foci and fibers were only observed in the confined fraction of the cell.
source: In cells that were trapped at the border of the micropillars used for confinement and were thus only confined over part of their area, myosin II foci and fibers were only observed in the confined fraction of the cell (Figure 4E), suggesting that confinement and cellular deformation are sensed locally within cells (rather than by a central sensor such as the nucleus, as in vertebrate cells [Lomakin et al., 2020; Venturini et al., 2020]).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Confinement and cellular deformation are sensed locally within S. rosetta cells rather than by a central sensor such as the nucleus.
source: In cells that were trapped at the border of the micropillars used for confinement and were thus only confined over part of their area, myosin II foci and fibers were only observed in the confined fraction of the cell (Figure 4E), suggesting that confinement and cellular deformation are sensed locally within cells (rather than by a central sensor such as the nucleus, as in vertebrate cells [Lomakin et al., 2020; Venturini et al., 2020]).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that myosin II redistribution occurs only in confined parts of partially confined cells

claim: In blebbing S. rosetta cells, myosin II was absent from expanding blebs, but re-invaded blebs prior to retraction.
source: In blebbing cells, myosin II was absent from expanding blebs, but re-invaded blebs prior to retraction, similar to F-actin (Figure 4F; Video 9 and Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F, Video 9, and Figure 4—video 1

claim: In unconfined flagellated S. rosetta cells, cortical microtubules radiated from the apical basal body to form a cage underneath the entire plasma membrane.
source: In unconfined flagellated S. rosetta cells, we observed that cortical microtubules radiated from the apical basal body to form a cage underneath the entire plasma membrane, as previously reported (Karpov and Leadbeater, 1998; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2013a; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-D and citations to Karpov and Leadbeater, 1998 and Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2013a

claim: In amoeboid S. rosetta cells, the microtubule cage remained present but mostly detached from the plasma membrane and around the nucleus.
source: In amoeboid cells, this cage remained present – but mostly detached from the plasma membrane and around the nucleus (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E-H

claim: Depletion of both intracellular and extracellular calcium did not reduce blebbing in response to confinement in S. rosetta.
source: Even after depletion of both intracellular and extracellular calcium, we observed no reduction in blebbing in response to confinement (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: Calcium signaling does not appear to be required for confinement-induced blebbing in S. rosetta.
source: Thus, despite the mechanistic similarities among choanoflagellates, animal cells, and slime molds in their reliance on actomyosin activity for bleb formation, calcium signaling does not appear to be required for confinement-induced blebbing in S. rosetta.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: S. rosetta cells that were initially confined less than 15 μm away from a pillar border were capable of escaping to a 3.5 μm deep space.
source: Cells that were initially confined less than 15 μm away from a pillar border were capable of escaping to a 3.5 μm deep space (Figure 5K; Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5K and Figure 5—video 1

claim: Escaping S. rosetta cells reliably elongated during escape.
source: Automated cell segmentation followed by morphometric quantification confirmed that escaping cells reliably elongated (Figure 5M; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Figure 5—video 2), while non-escaping cells (that never detected a border) remained nearly round (Figure 5N), indicating that this escape behavior involves specific cell shape changes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5M, 5N, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and Figure 5—video 2

claim: Treatment with blebbistatin dramatically reduced the escape behavior in S. rosetta.
source: Finally, treatment with blebbistatin dramatically reduced the escape behavior (Figure 5O), consistent with this behavior requiring myosin activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5O

claim: Five of six additional choanoflagellate species tested displayed blebbing activity under 2 μm confinement.
source: We tested the effect of 2 μm confinement on six additional choanoflagellate species that together represent the main branches of the choanoflagellate phylogenetic tree (Carr et al., 2017). All displayed blebbing activity under confinement (Figure 6A–J) with the exception of Diaphanoeca grandis (Figure 6K and L; Figure 6—video 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-J

claim: Diaphanoeca grandis did not display blebbing activity under 2 μm confinement.
source: All displayed blebbing activity under confinement (Figure 6A–J) with the exception of Diaphanoeca grandis (Figure 6K and L; Figure 6—video 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6K-L and Figure 6—video 1

claim: Choanoeca flexa sheet colonies dissociate into single cells that bleb and migrate over short distances without retracting their flagella.
source: The least pronounced response was seen in Choanoeca flexa (Figure 6G–H), whose sheet colonies (Brunet et al., 2019) dissociate into single cells that bleb and migrate over short distances without retracting their flagella, thus keeping an amoeboflagellate phenotype.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G-H

claim: Monosiga brevicollis showed a similar response to S. rosetta under confinement, including blebs and flagellar retraction.
source: Two other species, Monosiga brevicollis (Figure 6E–F; Video 12) and Acanthoeca spectabilis (Figure 6I–J; Video 13), showed a similar response to S. rosetta, including blebs and flagellar retraction.

claim: Acanthoeca spectabilis showed a similar response to S. rosetta under confinement, including blebs and flagellar retraction.
